- Model consistently overestimates prices in the short term (1-3 days) after recent spikes, especially when sentiment is bullish (≥0.67) — apply downward bias correction by 1-3% for the next 3-5 days.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+5% from prior day), model tends to overshoot and fail to account for subsequent mean reversion — reduce forecast by 2-5% for the next 5-7 days if sentiment turns neutral or bearish.
- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.8) and price is rising, model often fails to anticipate downward correction — add a 1-3% downward adjustment for the next 3-7 days if true outcome shows divergence.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.3) and model forecasts are rising, reduce forecast by 2-4% for the next 5-10 days — especially if recent history shows volatility or downward momentum.
- Model underestimates price drops after a strong bullish run — if sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.3–0.67) and true outcome shows a sharp drop, apply a 1-3% upward adjustment to forecast for the next 3-5 days.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to smooth out volatility — if true outcome shows a sharp spike or drop, adjust forecast to reflect recent sentiment and volatility, especially if sentiment is strong in the last 5 days.
- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over last 5 days, model tends to overestimate — reduce forecast by 1-3% for next 3-5 days.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.3) and price is falling, model often underestimates the drop — increase forecast downward by 1-3% for next 3-5 days.
- Model fails to account for event-driven volatility — if there’s a major event (e.g., policy change, market intervention), adjust forecast by ±2-5% based on sentiment direction and event impact.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often underestimates the magnitude of mean reversion — if sentiment is neutral or bearish and price is above 80, reduce forecast by 1-3% for next 5-7 days.
